name: Bite reclamation
lead: Bite reclamation is a term used in cosmetic dentistry for reopening the bite to restore vertical dimension lost through wear, such as from grinding or acid reflux, which can make the lower face look shortened.[1] It is described as part of full-mouth reconstruction, complex work involving many teeth.[1]

The looks payoff is the lower third of the face and the teeth themselves. Vertical dimension of occlusion is the up-and-down relationship of the jaws when the teeth meet, and dental references describe a deficient vertical dimension as giving a collapsed look with the chin close to the nose.[2] Rebuilding worn teeth to a greater height restores tooth length and lower-face height, which is why the procedure appears in hardmaxxing discussions of jaw and smile aesthetics.

Tooth wear has several causes, including attrition from grinding or clenching and erosion from acid, and wear can alter the occlusal vertical dimension.[3] A long-term study of severely worn dentitions rebuilt with direct composite at an increased vertical dimension followed patients for up to 11 years.[4]

angle.text: Patients with teeth worn short by grinding or acid have them rebuilt with composite or ceramic restorations, which restores tooth length and the height of the lower face. It is typically planned as a full-mouth restorative case.

paras: Cosmetic dentistry sources describe worn teeth reducing vertical dimension and bite reclamation restoring it, as part of full-mouth reconstruction.[1] Vertical dimension of occlusion (VDO), also called occlusal vertical dimension, is the up-and-down relationship between the upper and lower jaw when the teeth are in maximum intercuspation.[2]

Dentists assess it through several cues. Phonetics uses sibilant and fricative sounds, which depend on how close the incisors come; esthetics looks at nose, lip and chin configuration; the rest position of the jaw is recorded after the patient says 'Emma'; and a facial-proportion rule compares the distance from inner eye corner to lip corner with the distance between nose base and chin tip.[2]

Wikipedia's description of vertical dimension says that a correct VDO gives a normal nose, lip and chin configuration, a deficient one gives a collapsed-looking mouth with the chin too close to the nose, and an excessive one gives strained lip closure as if something were stuffed in the mouth.[2] The aesthetic aim of restoring height is therefore a lower face that is neither over-closed nor strained, with teeth of natural length.

Tooth wear is loss of tooth substance from causes other than decay and is usually multifactorial. Attrition comes from tooth-to-tooth contact and habits such as bruxism; erosion comes from acid in foods, drinks or reflux conditions such as GERD.[3] Severe wear can reduce tooth height and destabilise the bite, and the occlusal vertical dimension may change as a result.[3]

Wikipedia calls tooth wear very common, reporting that it affects about 97 percent of the population to some degree, and describes abrasion (for example from vigorous brushing or abrasive toothpaste) as a further cause.[3] Wear is scored with indices such as the Basic Erosive Wear Examination (Bartlett and colleagues, 2008) and the Tooth Wear Index (Smith and Knight, 1984).[3]

Dental references describe first identifying and controlling the cause, applying preventive measures and reviewing the patient for six to twelve months before restoration is considered.[3] Options for restoring lost height include increasing the vertical dimension, occlusal adjustment, crown lengthening or orthodontic extrusion, and the Dahl approach, in which the bite is propped open so worn teeth extrude.[3]

The Dahl approach is described as the most common method for gaining space: the bite is propped open so that worn teeth extrude relative to the rest, followed by direct or indirect restorations; pulp vitality is checked first because severely worn teeth may be non-vital.[3] Three scenarios are described: wear with loss of vertical dimension (common), wear without loss but with space (rare) and wear without loss but with limited space because of dentoalveolar compensation.[3]

A 2021 clinical study in the Journal of Clinical Medicine followed 13 patients with severely worn dentitions whose 164 teeth were rebuilt with direct microhybrid (first cohort, 59 teeth) or nanofilled (second cohort, 105 teeth) composite at an increased vertical dimension of occlusion, using a wax-up-based template technique. Patients were examined after a mean of 10.7 years (first cohort) or 5.2 years (second cohort) using USPHS criteria, and satisfaction was recorded on visual analogue scales. Overall restoration quality was good, nanofilled composite showed less surface degradation and better margins, and unfavorable events occurred in 13 of 59 restorations in the first cohort (ten repairable) and 23 of 105 in the second.[4]

Bite reclamation appears in hardmaxxing discussion of jaw and smile aesthetics as a restorative route to longer teeth and a restored lower face, mostly by analogy with cosmetic dental work rather than as a stand-alone procedure.[1]

card.summary: Rebuilding worn teeth to restore bite height; sources are thin and no trials were found.
card.note: Large restorative work; little published evidence located.

quick.overview:
Bite reclamation reopens a bite that has collapsed from tooth wear, to restore the height of the lower face. It is described as part of complex full-mouth reconstruction.

Only brief encyclopedic descriptions were found; no trials.
quick.mechanism: Worn teeth are rebuilt so the jaws meet at a greater vertical dimension.
quick.risks: Sources describe the work as complex; no safety data specific to the procedure were found.
